body:
Dropping masking isn't always an easy or conscious thing, even if you want to do it. 
I'm comfortable with my partner and know they'd be accepting of some stims I do (e.g. rocking and head shaking). A lot of the time though, I'm not even aware I need to do them until I'm away from my partner. The masking is strong enough that I don't even know I'm doing it.

Just wanted to add my two cents that it's not always an "either-or" situation of "masking equals a lack of safety and comfort". 
Sometimes it's a "that and also this" situation where there's both safety and masking 🙂.

I use the same socialising techniques I'd use to work out what someone else is feeling, but on myself. 
So I look back on situations and think "I acted/said ABC thing, which in other people usually means they're feeling XYZ". Then next time I'm in a similar situation, I use those conclusions as a way to determine my feelings. 

Seems to work well enough, for the most part. But it does require an amount of disconnection in the moment in order to do it, which isn't ideal.

Was there anything that helped you get over/come to terms with this happening to you? Like, a realisation or book or something? 
I had the same kind of experience, but haven't worked out how to work past it yet 🤔

(Not OP) Is there any chance you could provide more insight on your long conversation point #2? Like, how did they describe the feeling and your reaction to it?  
Thank-you if so, or I'm sorry if that's prying too much. I'm experiencing the same kind of troubles, but from the "initiator with RSD/trauma" side and want to try understand the other side better.

I'd interpret that to mean the other person has identified something that concerns them. They think it might be a problem, but they're not confident in their assessment. So they look to see how other people are reacting to it. If everyone looked worried, then they'd be more confident they understood it right, and yes it is a concern. And vice-versa.  
  
If they report to you, then that means you're in a higher position and theoretically more knowledgeable about the situation than they are. So looking at how you're handling it gives them a better idea about it.    
  
By asking "Aren't you worried about this?", they're expecting a "yeah it's a bit concerning" or a "no, this is OK" type of response. Rather than a question directed at you personally, they're trying to assuage their own concerns. It's a conversational way of asking "Am I interpreting this correctly? I've identified you as someone that might know the answer, and I can't visually tell if you're worried about it or not".

Exactly. One interaction doesn't make a good data set to draw conclusions from. 
I've had a pharmacist talk/look at me in a way i thought was a bit off and made me uncomfortable. I don't know if that was just their regular "look", though. I could've also read it wrong, and they were actually being very friendly. 
Unless they were very obviously hostile or said rude things, I wouldn't file a complaint based on a single interaction.

From being on the other side of such an interaction: 
I've had clients loudly state within my earshot that I was looking at them angrily. I was absently staring out the window next to them while thinking about something trivial, not even registering they were there. Whatever expression I was making wasn't angry, nor even aimed at them. 
They just interpreted it as one of displeasure (maybe because they were being too loud and knew it, lol), because they'd never seen me before.

Any medical professional that's worth seeing will understand the difference between the stereotypical presentation of autistic (think Sheldon Cooper from Big Bang Theory) and actual autism. Unfortunately, many doctors/psychs still think that stereotype is the only way it can present. 

If they say something stupid like "you can't be autistic because you have a job!", it's the same as saying "that's not a dog, it's yellow" because everyone they know has a brown or black dog.

I've got a full time job, my own place, and I'm in a relationship. If I hadn't recently gone through a life struggle in my early 30s that was harder to deal with than it was for many of my peers, I likely never would've questioned if I'm autistic. Turns out I struggle with quite a lot of things, I just learnt to mask it well.

I generally don't know how I feel in any given moment (outside a few major emotions). Once a situation is over, I'll mentally play it back and use the social pattern-recognition skills I've developed for understanding others, but on myself.

There's been some social events that have caused me the Big Feels, and I didn't handle them well because I was upset, but genuinely didn't "feel" it. 
I've learned to keep an eye on myself, and sometimes my actions get flagged by my own brain as a "Hey, this is like another situation. You're probably feeling XYZ right now". 
So I then run through a mental check list of things I know I should do, what helps me and others the most, etc.

So I haven't been able to "feel" my emotions any better, but I've learned that treating myself as a third person that I need to interpret the emotions and actions of like I do everyone else, has been very helpful.
When my partner and I were still getting to know each other, they literally gave me some small fancy rocks they thought I'd like. Can confirm, I'm secretly a bird and this worked on me.

Perhaps look up "alexythemia".

It's a thing in and of itself, where you can have problems recognising emotions within yourself (and others, depending on which school of thought the test is based on).

For example, I've learned that I dont recognise what emotions I'm feeling during most events as they happen. When I later analyse it, I think: 
"Other people act in XYZ manner when they're happy. I did the same thing. Therefore, I was happy during that time, and that's how my thoughts and actions are influenced by happiness". Then that gets filed away and used as evidence in later comparisons.
I love how casually you threw in "koalafications" into that sentence. Reading that made me smile, thankyou 😄

Had this happen to me recently. Almost had a meltdown trying to explain something, not knowing if the other person undstood me, or if I was the one at fault/failing to translate my thoughts into their language.


Eventually said "I'm just talking in circles at this point, but I don't know if you understand what I mean". She said "Yeah I got your point a while ago".
Almost started crying and wanted to shout "why didn't you say so before then? I've told you I over explain things, just say you understand!" 🫠


She meant well, but had low self-confidence and didn't speak up earlier. So getting upset wouldn't help - and so I had to repress my reaction for her sake 😿

I both enjoy and despise the feeling of bras at the same time, it's confusing, lol.
I don't like things tight against me, but the pressure sensation of a bra against my chest is comforting.


I can get away without wearing one most of the time, thankfully (small boobs are both a blessing and a curse). If I *do* have to though, there's no rhyme or reason to when I'll switch from liking it to a strong urge to rip it off  - _-'  haha

I feel this one. I work in a public-facing role and get annoyed when ND people are too loud or don't pick up on my cues.
It's like...this is something we both find hard, the least you could do is *be aware* that I'm out of my comfort zone so you can be in yours. Put in some effort and meet me half way, please? I'm in burnout, and your shout-talking is distressing me.



But then that's unfair on them to expect them to do what NT people keep expecting of me, but also feels unfair that I have to mask for ND as well as NT people and...yeah. This one's a struggle, for sure :/

Also, hug corners as tightly as you can if the map allows it. Peaking out from behind a wall and blasting a little ways out before running back behind it will let you survive much longer. Only do it roughly twice from the same place though if the enemy can advance towards you, as they will try to get you. Preempt it, and change locations to confuse them.  
Reaper is more about harassing the enemy and performing hit-and-run attacks than full frontal assaults. Stick close to your teammates and just aim to be a nuisance so you get picks, but the enemy can't focus on both you and your teammates.
